title: Language core: collections internals, generics and type hints
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: HashMap buckets, resize and treeify, ArrayList vs LinkedList vs ArrayDeque, TreeMap, CME traps, Python dict/list/set/deque, Java generics (bounds, wildcards, erasure) and Python typing.
source: OpenJDK HashMap source and JEP 180; Java Collections Framework docs; Oracle Java Tutorials: Generics; Python docs: data structures, typing; Baeldung; Real Python

questions.prompt: A new HashMap<>() has the default capacity of 16 and load factor 0.75. Counting from 1, which put of a new distinct key makes the table resize for the first time?
questions.explanation: Threshold = 16 x 0.75 = 12. The resize runs when the size exceeds the threshold, so the 13th insertion doubles the table to 32 (HashMap.putVal: if (++size > threshold) resize()).

questions.prompt: Since Java 8 a long collision chain in a HashMap bin can be converted into a red-black tree, but only if the table capacity is at least some minimum; below it the table is resized instead. What is that minimum capacity (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY)?
questions.explanation: TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 (chain length), UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6, MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64. Trees give O(log n) worst-case lookups for Comparable keys instead of O(n).

questions.prompt: Match each structure to its defining property.

right.text: Resizable array: O(1) get(i), amortised O(1) append, O(n) insert in the middle
Doubly linked nodes: O(1) unlink at a known node but O(n) get(i)
Circular array: O(1) at both ends, no null elements
Red-black tree: sorted keys, O(log n) get/put
Doubly linked blocks: O(1) append/popleft, O(n) indexing in the middle

questions.explanation: In practice ArrayList and ArrayDeque win on cache locality; LinkedList is rarely the right answer because get(i) walks the nodes and every element costs an allocation.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: ArrayDeque is usually a better choice than LinkedList for a stack or a queue in Java.
questions.reason: ArrayDeque stores elements in a contiguous circular array and allocates no node object per element.

whys.a: Correct: less memory, better cache locality and no per-node allocation make it faster in typical use.
whys.b: R is not only true but is the main reason for A.
whys.c: R is true: the implementation is a resizable circular array.
whys.d: A is true; the Javadoc says ArrayDeque is likely faster than Stack as a stack and than LinkedList as a queue.

questions.explanation: ArrayDeque rejects null elements and is not thread-safe. Prefer it over the legacy Stack class and over LinkedList for queues.

questions.prompt: Write one Java statement or a short loop that removes all even numbers from a List<Integer> named nums without throwing ConcurrentModificationException.

checks.label: uses removeIf or an explicit Iterator.remove

questions.explanation: removeIf is the idiom. An explicit Iterator with it.remove() is equally valid; a for-each loop that calls nums.remove(...) is the bug being avoided.

options.why: Correct: remove(Object) deletes 2; size becomes 2 and the cursor is already 2, so hasNext() is false and no check for modification ever runs.
This is the usual result, but here hasNext() returns false before next() can call checkForComodification().
The element is removed from the list; nothing restores it.
Only the element equal to 2 is removed, and the loop ends rather than removing more.

questions.explanation: Fail-fast iterators check modCount in next(), not in hasNext(). Removing the second-to-last element is the one case that silently works; removing the first would throw. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: In Python 3.7 and later, a dict iterates its keys in insertion order as part of the language guarantee.

options.why: Correct: this became a language guarantee in 3.7 (an implementation detail of CPython 3.6).
It is guaranteed, not just a CPython quirk; collections.OrderedDict only adds extras like move_to_end and order-sensitive equality.

questions.explanation: CPython keeps a compact entries array plus a sparse index table. Mutating a dict while iterating it raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about CPython dictionaries.
questions.text: CPython implements a dict as a {1} table that resolves collisions with {2} addressing (probing), so a lookup is {3} on average.
questions.explanation: Java HashMap chains colliding entries in a bin (list or tree); CPython probes other slots in the same table. Keys must be hashable, which is why lists cannot be dict keys.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A List<String> can be passed where a List<Object> is expected in Java.
questions.reason: String is a subtype of Object.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can be right.
whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: generics are invariant, so List<String> is not a List<Object> (use List<? extends Object> or List<?>), even though String extends Object.

questions.explanation: Invariance exists so that you cannot add an Integer through a List<Object> alias to a list that really holds strings. Arrays are covariant and pay for it with ArrayStoreException.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about Java generics and type erasure.

options.why: Correct: the type arguments are erased, so both are the same runtime class.

options.text: Inside class Box<T>, the expression new T() does not compile.
options.why: Correct: T is erased to Object (or its bound), so the runtime has no idea which class to instantiate.

options.text: Inside class Box<T>, the expression new T[10] does not compile.
options.why: Correct: generic array creation is rejected because arrays need the reified element type.

options.text: void f(List<String>) and void f(List<Integer>) can be declared as overloads in one class.
options.why: Both erase to f(List), a name clash compile error.

options.text: A primitive such as int can be used as a type argument: List<int>.
options.why: Type arguments must be reference types; use List<Integer>.

questions.explanation: Erasure replaces type variables with their bound (Object by default) and inserts casts; generics exist only at compile time. Workarounds: pass a Class<T> token, or use a Supplier<T>.

questions.prompt: Write a static generic Java method max that takes a non-empty List<T>, where T is bounded so its elements can be compared, and returns the largest element.

checks.label: declares a bounded type parameter T extends Comparable
compares elements with compareTo (or a Comparator)
method is called max and takes a List/Collection

questions.explanation: The most general signature is <T extends Comparable<? super T>>. A stream with Collections.max(list) is the one-liner; alternative implementations that satisfy the bound are accepted.

questions.prompt: Given void copy(List<? extends Number> src, List<? super Integer> dst), which statement compiles inside the method?

options.why: Correct: a List<? super Integer> is a consumer; any Integer fits whatever supertype list it really is.
src may be a List<Double>; the compiler cannot allow any add except null.
dst could be a List<Number> or List<Object>, so get only promises Object.
dst could be a List<Object>, so a Number is not guaranteed; only Object is.

questions.explanation: PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Read from ? extends, write to ? super. (Verified by compiling it.)

questions.prompt: Write a Python function first(items) with type hints using a TypeVar named T so that mypy infers the element type of the sequence it returns.

checks.label: parameter is a Sequence/list of T

questions.explanation: On Python 3.12+ you can write def first[T](items: Sequence[T]) -> T. Type hints are not enforced at runtime; mypy or pyright check them statically.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Since Java 8 a HashMap with many colliding Comparable keys keeps lookups at O(log n) instead of O(n).
questions.reason: TreeMap keeps its keys in sorted order.

whys.a: R is true but it describes TreeMap, not the in-bin trees; it does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is about a different class. Treeified bins are red-black trees, though a plain HashMap iteration order stays unsorted.
whys.c: R is a true statement about TreeMap.
whys.d: A is true: that is the point of treeification (JEP 180).

questions.explanation: JEP 180 improved HashMap under heavy collisions, notably hash-flooding attacks. The tree uses hashCode then compareTo or a tie-breaker.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: collections.deque.popleft() takes O(1) time, whereas list.pop(0) takes O(n).
questions.reason: A Python list is implemented as a doubly linked list of nodes.

whys.a: R is false: a list is a dynamic array of pointers.
whys.b: R is false, so option b cannot hold.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the list shifts every remaining pointer); R is false because CPython lists are arrays of pointers (that is why index access is O(1)).
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Use deque for queues (BFS); a list is fine for stacks (append/pop at the end).
